blocks.html: He could not have addressed himself better, inasmuch as friends, kinsfolk, household servants and neighbours are those who commonly know and understand the acts of the persons to whom they belong by right of kinship, friendship, familiarity or neighbourhood. Kinsfolk (say our Jurisconsults) have knowledge, in all likelihood, of what their kinsfolk do, of their estate, condition and quality a; and so likewise do neighbours among themselves b: so that he who says he does not know the estate or the deeds of his kinsman or neighbour cannot be excused under the pretext of the ignorance that he alleges c. Which must be understood to be true of things which in all likelihood fall within the knowledge of a kinsman or a neighbour: such as the health or the age of a kinsman d, the poverty or wealth e, dwelling f, marriage g, reputation and renown h of a neighbour; and generally all acts which cannot be done, dispatched or properly carried through save by the succession of time, requiring some length and interval i. For the things which are done among kinsfolk or in the neighbourhood, and can be brought very soon to an end and completed in a little time, do not easily pass into the knowledge of the other kinsfolk and neighbours, because they are most often done secretly — as a contract, a will, a crime k. For even what is done in public once only is not to be presumed to be known by all persons, seeing that such an act has had no duration l; although it is commonly said that of what is done in public no one may allege or pretend ignorance m.

notes.gloss: D. 43.12.2: a river is told from a brook by its size "or by the estimation of those who live round about"; C. 5.4.9: a marriage kept "with the neighbours or others knowing of it" is a true marriage though no instruments were drawn — the neighbours' knowledge as proof.

notes.gloss: A notice limiting a manager's authority must be posted plainly and permanently; one posted and then taken down binds no one — the law Coras draws on for "such an act has had no duration".

notes.citation: Decretals, X 4.18 (Qui matrimonium accusare possunt), c. Cum in tua (X 4.18.6); and § Proscribere (D. 14.3.11.3), at its beginning, already cited at {l}

notes.gloss: For the common saying that no one may plead ignorance of what is done in public; preſcribere is a wrong sort for proſcribere.
